extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary critics, and students of fiction/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance on plotting, characterization, and the use of fantasy in the novel — what makes a plot succeed or fail, how incidents should relate to characters, and how and when to demand extra suspension of disbelief for fantastic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot ought to cause surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: This shock, followed by the feeling, 'Oh, that's all right,' is a sign that all is well with the plot: characters, to be real, ought to run smoothly, but a plot ought to cause surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use incidents that produce genuine shocks or unexpected reversals which then illuminate or reorient reader (and characters). Example: the horse-whipping of Dr. Shrapnel in Beauchamp's Career gives a shock that transforms the book's personages. A successful plot moment should both surprise and then make sense in retrospect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should spring from character and alter character
rubrics_metrics.description: Incident springs out of character, and having occurred it alters that character. People and events are closely connected, and he does it by means of these contrivances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure plot events feel rooted in what characters would plausibly do or provoke; contrivances are permissible only when they grow naturally from character and then react upon them. Anti-pattern: plot devices that feel imposed from outside (contrivances that don't spring from characters) weaken realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrivances are acceptable if they derive from character
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essentially a contrivance, a door through which the book is made to pass, emerging in an altered form... contrivances that spring from the characters and react upon them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An episodic or loosely knit plot (a series of contrivances/kiosks) can succeed if each contrivance is artfully placed and motivated by character. Meredith's plots are praised for such contrivances; the contrivance should transform the world of the book rather than feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let plot dominate or force characters against their natures
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a plot triumphs too completely. The characters have to suspend their natures at every turn, or else are so swept away by the course of Fate that our sense of their reality is weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid designing events that compel characters to act implausibly or unnaturally simply to serve plot requirements; maintain characters' internal consistency and vitality even when plot imposes strong demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-emphasis on rigid causality or fate
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy arranges events with emphasis on causality... he has emphasized causality more strongly than his medium permits... the characters have been required to contribute too much to the plot; except in their rustic humours, their vitality has been impoverished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of conceiving the novel as a machine of hammer-strokes where characters are chained to fate; excessive prioritizing of causa/events over character reduces realism and emotional engagement. Balance causal design with lifelike characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endings should not be mechanical wind-ups that kill character vitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Nearly all novels are feeble at the end. This is because the plot requires to be wound up... the characters go dead while he is at work, and our final impression of them is through deadness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived dénouements where incidents and people are forced into the service of a tidy ending (stock devices like death and marriage often used as conveniences). Strive to preserve character life and avoid a 'bookish' wind-up that betrays earlier vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: A plot needs mystery that is later resolved
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot, then, is the novel in its logical intellectual aspect: it requires mystery, but the mysteries are solved later on: the reader may be moving about in worlds unrealized, but the novelist has no misgivings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mysteries (unexplained situations, withheld information) to sustain curiosity; resolution may come later and retroactively justify events. Mystery is a structural tool to keep the reader engaged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective concealment of a character’s inner development can be a valid device
rubrics_metrics.description: Meredith has concealed the change. It would have spoiled his high comedy if we had been kept in touch with it throughout... This is one of the countless examples in which either plot or character has to suffer, and Meredith with his unerring good sense here lets the plot triumph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withholding the reader's access to a character's inner change can create dramatic effect and preserve comedic or plot momentum. But misuse (e.g., Charlotte Brontë's concealment of Lucy Snowe's discovery) can harm perceived integrity of character; weigh costs to character realism before concealing facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider whether to plan the novel or let it grow
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is exciting and may be beautiful, yet is it not a fetish, borrowed from the drama... Cannot fiction devise a framework that is not so logical yet more suitable to its genius?... For a book of this type any plan would be unsuitable. The whole of it would go wrong if I decided any detail ahead. I am waiting for reality to dictate to me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide methodically whether you will pre-plan cause-and-effect structure or permit the book to develop organically. Both approaches are legitimate; choose based on the work's aims (e.g., tightly logical plot vs. open, exploratory fiction) and be conscious of the trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: The plot is not the only legitimate framework for the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is the novel in its logical intellectual aspect... why has a novel to be planned? Cannot it grow? Why need it close, as a play closes? Cannot it open out?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with alternatives to conventional plot (fragmented plots, diary-material, meta-fictional devices) when the novel's genius calls for opening out rather than closing. Example: Gide's Les Faux Monnayeurs mixes fragments, diaries, and authorial self-questioning to challenge the plot's primacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy asks readers to 'pay something extra' — accept the book and its particular oddities
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy asks us to pay something extra. It compels us to an adjustment that is different to an adjustment required by a work of art... The fantasist says, 'Here’s something that could not occur. I must ask you first to accept my book as a whole, and secondly to accept certain things in my book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including fantastic elements, acknowledge that you demand an additional suspension of disbelief. Make that demand pay off: either delight readers who 'pay the sixpence' or accept that some readers will stop reading. Be explicit about the book's terms and maintain internal logic that justifies the extra ask.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy is distinguished by its mythology and a 'beam of light' cutting across other aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: We shall give that bar of light two names, fantasy and prophecy... I mean something that cuts across them like a bar of light, that is intimately connected with them at one place and patiently illumines all their problems, and at another place shoots over or through them as if they did not exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a unifying imaginative principle (myth, deity, leitmotif) that transfigures ordinary elements of the novel. Fantasy's inventiveness often hinges on such an axis (Hermes, fairies, Muddle) which reshapes perception rather than simply adding supernatural facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and deploy the limited set of fantasy devices creatively
rubrics_metrics.description: Devices which writers of a fantastic turn have used—such as the introduction of a god, ghost, angel, monkey, monster, midget, witch into ordinary life; or the introduction of ordinary men into no man’s land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; or divings into and dividings of personality; or finally the device of parody or adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fantasy relies on a recognisable but finite toolkit; freshness comes from novel combinations, temperament, and precise execution. Choose devices that suit authorial temperament and the book’s aim, and avoid mere novelty for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy may be improvisational in air but still requires solid character-drawing and moral/critical substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of fantasy penetrates into every corner of the universe... They may contain solid character-drawing, penetrating and bitter criticism of conduct and civilization; yet our simile of the beam of light must remain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't let the playfulness or 'improvised' quality of fantasy excuse weak characterization or shallow thematic content. Successful fantasy often combines whimsical or supernatural dress with rigorous characterisation and insightful critique (example: Flecker's Magic—fantastic events paired with individual character grip).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fantasy from prophecy by the nature of their mythologies and aims
rubrics_metrics.description: They are alike in having gods, and unlike in the gods they have... By their mythologies we shall distinguish these two sorts of novels... When we come to prophecy, we shall utter no invocation, but it will have been to whatever transcends our abilities...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the work's mythic elements aim at playful/medieval-like fantasy (fauns, dryads, Hermes) or at prophetic, transcendent claims (religious, prophetic deities). The choice affects tone, seriousness, and what demands you make on the reader.
